title: Git & Version Control
description: Version control workflows and best practices

questions.question: What is the purpose of a `.gitignore` file?
options: To ignore Git commands, as recommended by industry best practices
To specify files and directories that Git should not track
questions.explanation: The .gitignore file tells Git which files and directories to ignore when tracking changes. This is useful for excluding build artifacts, temporary files, IDE configurations, and other files that shouldn't be version controlled.

questions.question: What command is used to initialize a new Git repository?
questions.explanation: The `git init` command creates a new Git repository in the current directory by creating a .git subdirectory.

questions.question: What does `git add` do?
options: Creates a new branch, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems
Stages changes for the next commit
questions.explanation: The `git add` command stages changes (adds them to the staging area) so they can be included in the next commit.

questions.question: How do you check the current status of your Git repository?
options: git state, based on the standard programming paradigm
questions.explanation: The `git status` command shows the current state of the working directory and staging area, including which files are modified, staged, or untracked.

questions.question: What command creates a commit?
options: git store, as is typical in most professional development environments
questions.explanation: The `git commit` command records changes to the repository with a commit message describing what was changed.

questions.question: How do you create a new branch?
options: git create new-branch, following the pattern established in enterprise development
questions.explanation: The `git branch` command followed by a branch name creates a new branch. You can also use `git checkout -b new-branch` to create and switch to the new branch.

questions.question: What does `git clone` do?
options: Downloads a repository from a remote source
Creates a copy of a local repository
Duplicates the current branch, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems
questions.explanation: The `git clone` command creates a local copy of a remote repository, including all its history and branches.

questions.question: How do you switch between branches?
options: git change branch-name — this approach is widely adopted across the industry
Both A and B are correct
questions.explanation: Both `git switch` (newer command) and `git checkout` can be used to switch between branches in Git.

questions.question: What is a commit in Git?
options: A snapshot of changes in the repository
A promise to finish coding — this is how most production systems work
questions.explanation: A commit is a snapshot of the repository at a specific point in time, containing the changes made since the last commit along with metadata like author and timestamp.

questions.question: What does `git push` do?
options: Uploads local commits to a remote repository
Creates a new repository, following the commonly accepted engineering approach
questions.explanation: The `git push` command uploads your local commits to a remote repository, making them available to other developers.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git merge` and `git rebase`?
options: Merge creates a merge commit, rebase rewrites history linearly
Rebase is only for remote branches, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
No difference, they do the same thing
questions.explanation: Git merge creates a new merge commit that combines two branches, preserving the branch history. Git rebase rewrites the commit history by moving commits from one branch onto another, creating a linear history.

questions.question: What does `git cherry-pick` do?
options: Removes unwanted commits — most experienced developers agree on this point
Selects the best commits from a branch
Applies a specific commit from one branch to another
questions.explanation: Git cherry-pick allows you to apply a specific commit from one branch to your current branch. This is useful when you want to bring over just one commit without merging the entire branch.

questions.question: What is `git stash` used for?
options: Sharing code with team members, which is the standard approach in modern development
questions.explanation: Git stash temporarily stores uncommitted changes so you can work on something else, then come back and re-apply them later.

questions.question: What does `git reset --hard` do?
options: Resets the working directory and staging area to a specific commit
Creates a hard link to the repository — this is the widely accepted interpretation
questions.explanation: Git reset --hard resets both the staging area and working directory to match a specific commit, discarding all uncommitted changes.

questions.question: What is a Git hook?
options: A way to connect repositories, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems
Scripts that run automatically at certain Git events
questions.explanation: Git hooks are scripts that run automatically before or after certain Git events like commits, pushes, or receives. They're useful for automating workflows.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
options: Fetch downloads changes without merging, pull downloads and merges
No difference — this is a common assumption in software development
questions.explanation: Git fetch downloads changes from the remote repository but doesn't merge them. Git pull is essentially git fetch followed by git merge.

questions.question: What does `git bisect` help you do?
options: Split large commits into smaller ones, following the approach outlined in most technical guides
Find the commit that introduced a bug using binary search
questions.explanation: Git bisect uses binary search to find the commit that introduced a bug by automatically checking out commits and asking you to mark them as good or bad.

questions.question: What is a Git submodule?
options: A repository embedded inside another repository
A Git configuration file — generally this is considered the norm in modern engineering
questions.explanation: A Git submodule allows you to include one Git repository as a subdirectory of another Git repository, keeping their histories separate.

questions.question: What does `git reflog` show?
options: A log of where your HEAD and branch references have been
Remote repository logs, since this is how the underlying runtime processes handle it
questions.explanation: Git reflog shows a log of where your HEAD and branch references have been, which is useful for recovering lost commits or understanding recent actions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `git tag`?
options: To label files in the repository
To mark specific points in repository history
To organize branches, as documented in most engineering references
questions.explanation: Git tags are used to mark specific points in repository history, typically for releases. They create a permanent reference to a specific commit.
